a photographic essay, EDUC90006

Three Skies

Before this subject, I photographed a lot of skies without asking why. Looking back at three years of ordinary photographs from three places I've lived, I found a pattern I never noticed while I was living inside it. Touch each point to open what I found there.

Visit all three to see what connects them.

after visiting all three

One line, not three dots

None of these photographs were taken with theory in mind — they all predate this subject entirely. For most of the time I was taking them, each place existed as its own separate world: Thailand's ordinariness, Singapore's staged nature, Melbourne's chased skies, never held up against one another, because there was no reason to.

It is only from here, now, that I find myself wondering what the sky looked like above my grandmother's garden, or above the towers I grew up beneath — questions I never once asked while I was standing under those skies myself. Ingold (2000) argues that a lived world is a sphere, encompassing the person at its centre, revealed gradually rather than surveyed from without; it is only the act of moving on, of wayfaring from one place to the next, that lets the line connecting separate spheres become visible at all — and only from outside them.

I don't think I am uncovering three different relationships with environment. I think I am uncovering one relationship, seen for the first time as continuous, from the only vantage point distance ever allows — and I still can't tell whether that counts as insight, or just as a story I've learned to tell backwards.

references

Cronon, W. (1996). The trouble with wilderness: Or, getting back to the wrong nature. Environmental History, 1(1), 7–28.

Ingold, T. (2000). Globes and spheres: The topology of environmentalism. In The perception of the environment: Essays on livelihood, dwelling and skill (pp. 259–272). Routledge.
